content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Thanks — a bookmark app. Before we talk about any screens or features, I'd like to understand the goal behind it, so we build the right thing.

**When this is finished, what should be different from how things are for you now?**

For example — are you frustrated that bookmarks are scattered across browsers and you lose track of them? Are you trying to rediscover things you saved long ago? Or is it about sharing collections with other people? What's the itch you're trying to scratch?

Once I understand *why* you want this, I'll walk you through actual working screens one at a time so you can react to something concrete rather than just discussing it in the abstract.

I want to stop losing track of stuff I save. Right now I bookmark things in my browser and never find them again — it's just a giant messy pile. So mainly I want to save links and actually be able to find them later and keep them a bit organized.

content:
That's really helpful. Let me play back what I heard to make sure I've got the direction right:

Today, saving a link is easy but it goes into a pile you can never dig back out of. So the app isn't really about *saving* links — saving is the easy part. The real payoff is **being able to find something again later**, and keeping things organized enough that finding stays easy as the pile grows.

In other words, if the app let you save links beautifully but you still couldn't find things a month later, it would have failed. Does that sound like the heart of it?

One scope question, in plain terms: when you imagine "finally finding that thing I saved," how do you picture getting to it — searching by typing what you remember, browsing through neat groups/folders, or something else? (You don't have to be sure — I'll show you options later.)

And one more: **what kind of app do you picture using this as** — something in your web browser, a phone app, a desktop app, or something else?

Yeah, that's exactly it — if I save something and can't dig it back out later, it's useless. You nailed it.

For finding stuff, honestly probably a mix — sometimes I'd just type in what I remember and search for it, and sometimes I'd want to browse by some kind of category or label. Both, I think.

And I picture this in my web browser, on my computer.

**1. Open `prototypes/p03a-folders.html` — "Folders"**
Click **Travel** in the left sidebar. Notice each link sits in exactly **one** folder (see the little folder label on each). A link about "Tech travel gadgets" would have to go in *either* Travel *or* Tech, not both.

**2. Open `prototypes/p03b-tags.html` — "Tags"**
Click **Travel** in the left sidebar. Notice a single link can carry **several** labels — the Kyoto link is under both *Travel* and *Japan*, so it shows up when you browse either. You can also click a label chip right on a link.

Just click **Travel**. Here you never set anything up — **the app sorts links into topics by itself** based on the page. Notice the ✨ topic on each link was assigned automatically, with no work from you when saving.

A key thing I want you to weigh as you try them — this is the real trade-off:

- **Folders & Tags** give you full control over the grouping, but cost you a moment of effort per link (choosing a folder / adding labels when you save).
- **Automatic** costs you *zero* effort — matching how much you liked the frictionless paste-to-save — but the app decides the groupings, so sometimes it may file something where you wouldn't have.

The trade-off to feel here: **A** guarantees things get tagged but makes every single save heavier. **B** keeps saving dead-simple but relies on you to circle back (and we both know how "I'll organize it later" tends to go). **C** tries to get the best of both — instant save, plus a gentle in-the-moment nudge you can ignore.

Which feels right for how you'd actually use it? If you're between two, say so.

Open `prototypes/p07-delete.html`. Same list of 4 links; two buttons up top switch how deleting works. (If you delete everything, just click a mode button to reset.)

**Please try both:**

1. **"Confirm first"** (the default): click the 🗑 trash icon on any link. It turns into a **"Delete? [Delete] [Cancel]"** prompt right on that row — nothing is removed until you confirm. Try deleting one, and try cancelling one.

2. Now click **"Delete instantly, with Undo"** up top, then click the 🗑 on a link. It **vanishes immediately**, and a black **"Deleted — Undo"** bar appears at the bottom for about 5 seconds. Delete one, then click **Undo** to bring it back. Delete another and just let the bar fade to keep it gone.

The trade-off: **Confirm first** never lets a link disappear by accident, but you approve every single deletion (an extra click each time). **Delete + Undo** is faster and frictionless, and still protects you — but only for those few seconds before the bar fades.

Given you'll be clearing out old stuff fairly often to keep the pile tidy, which fits you better?

Delete instantly with Undo fits me better. If I'm clearing out a bunch of old stuff, confirming every single one gets tedious fast — the instant delete keeps it quick, and the few-second Undo bar is enough of a safety net in case I zap the wrong one. That one.

content:
We've now covered everything end-to-end, including the rough edges. Here's where we've landed — in plain terms, this is the app we've designed together:

**Saving**
- You save a link by pasting it and hitting Save — nothing else required.
- The app automatically grabs the page's real title (e.g. the article headline) so you can tell things apart later. If it can't get the title (page blocks it, or your wifi is down), it saves the link anyway and lets you give it a name yourself.
- If you try to save a link you already have, it won't make a duplicate — it points you to the one you saved.
- Pasting something that isn't a link is gently refused.

**Finding**
- Type in the search box and the list narrows live as you type — no Enter, no waiting — matching both the headline and the site.
- If nothing matches, it tells you and suggests trying different words.

**Organizing**
- Links are organized with tags, and a link can carry several — so it shows up under every label that fits.
- Right after you save, a quick prompt lets you tag the link on the spot (with autocomplete suggesting your existing tags), or skip it if you're rushing.
- Browse by clicking any tag to see everything under it.

**Cleaning up**
- Delete a link instantly with one click, with a few-second Undo in case you zap the wrong one.

**Deliberately left for later:** detecting dead links, and I've separately noted "keep search fast even with a huge collection" as a build-quality target.

That's **8 settled flows**. **May I now start building this scope for real?** (Nothing gets implemented until you say go — and if anything above feels off or missing, now's the moment to tell me.)
Yeah, that all sounds right to me — it covers what I came here for. Go ahead and build it.

Implementation is complete and **Phase 3 verification passed — 24/24 tests green**, including one acceptance test per approved scenario. Now for **Phase 4: your acceptance.** Rather than just telling you it's done, I'd like you to run it and confirm each behaviour matches what we agreed.

**Start the app:**
```
cd implementation
npm start
```
Then open **http://localhost:3000** in your browser. (First run shows the empty "No bookmarks yet" screen.)

Please walk these through — this is every flow we settled, in order:

1. **Save + real title (SCN-001):** Paste a real article link and hit Save. → It appears at the top; the actual page title fills in.
2. **Tag in the moment (SCN-004):** Right after saving, the "Add tags for this?" prompt is focused — type a few letters, pick a suggested/typed tag, add one or two, then move on (or hit skip).
3. **Save a few more**, tagging some, so you have a small pile.
4. **Live search (SCN-002):** Type in the search box — the list narrows as you type, matching headline or site, with matches highlighted.
5. **Browse by tag (SCN-003):** Click a tag on the left (or a chip on a link) — you see only links with that tag; click a link tagged two ways to confirm it shows under both. Click **All** to clear.
6. **Duplicate (SCN-006):** Paste a link you already saved → "You already saved this link" + "Show me the one I saved."
7. **Non-link (SCN-006):** Type `grocery list` and Save → gently refused, nothing saved.
8. **Delete + undo (SCN-008):** Click 🗑 on a link → it vanishes with a "Deleted — Undo" bar; click Undo to restore, or let it fade to keep it gone.

(The "title not found → add a name" and offline cases (SCN-006/007) trigger when a page blocks title-fetching or your wifi is down — you'll see a "title not found" flag with an "add a name" link when that happens.)

**Does the behaviour match what you intended across these flows?** If anything is off, tell me which step and I'll fix it (if it's an implementation gap) or revisit the scenario with you. Once you confirm, I'll record acceptance and close out the cycle.

I ran through all of them and it does everything I asked — saving pulls the real titles, the in-the-moment tagging is smooth, search narrows as I type, tags show a link under both labels, duplicates get caught, and delete-with-undo works. content:
🎉 **Cycle 1 complete and accepted.** Thank you — this was a good collaboration.

Here's where things stand:

**What we built** — a personal bookmark web app whose real job is *finding things again*, not just saving them:
- Paste-to-save with automatic real-title capture
- Live search across titles and sites
- Multi-tag organization with an in-the-moment tagging prompt
- Instant delete with an Undo safety net
- Graceful handling of empty states, duplicates, non-links, missing titles, and offline saves

**Status**
- 8 scenarios approved and accepted
- 24/24 automated tests passing (9 Gherkin acceptance tests + unit/integration)
- Zero dependencies — runs with just `cd implementation && npm start` → http://localhost:3000

**Artifacts on disk**
